questions.stem_md:
A four-sided die is loaded so that the probability of the score $j$ is $\dfrac{j^2}{30}$ for $j = 1, 2, 3, 4$. Find

(a) a check that this is a valid assignment of probabilities, [1]

(b) the probability of an even score, [1]

(c) the probability of a score of at least $3$, [1]

(d) the probability that the score is even or at least $3$, using the addition theorem. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Every value $\dfrac{j^2}{30}$ is positive and $\dfrac{1 + 4 + 9 + 16}{30} = \dfrac{30}{30} = 1$, so the assignment is valid.

(b) $P(\text{even}) = P(2) + P(4) = \dfrac{4}{30} + \dfrac{16}{30} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

(c) $P(\text{at least } 3) = P(3) + P(4) = \dfrac{9}{30} + \dfrac{16}{30} = \dfrac{5}{6}$.

(d) The score $4$ is both even and at least $3$, so $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{16}{30} = \dfrac{8}{15}$. Then $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{8}{15} = \dfrac{20 + 25 - 16}{30} = \dfrac{29}{30}$.

questions.solution_md: Check the total first; the later parts add the probabilities of the scores in each event, then use the overlap.

questions.stem_md:
A committee of four is chosen at random from $5$ teachers and $4$ students, every committee being equally likely. Find

(a) the number of possible committees, [1]

(b) the probability that it has exactly two teachers, [2]

(c) the probability that it has at least one student, using the complement. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n(S) = \dbinom{9}{4} = \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 126$.

(b) Two teachers and two students: $\dbinom{5}{2} \times \dbinom{4}{2} = 10 \times 6 = 60$ committees, so $P = \dfrac{60}{126} = \dfrac{10}{21}$.

(c) The complement is "no student", that is four teachers: $\dbinom{5}{4} = 5$ committees, with probability $\dfrac{5}{126}$. So $P(\text{at least one student}) = 1 - \dfrac{5}{126} = \dfrac{121}{126}$.

questions.solution_md: Use combinations for the committee; for at least one, count the committees with none and subtract.

questions.stem_md:
In an imagined school of $120$ pupils, $70$ take art, $55$ take music and $20$ take neither subject. A pupil is chosen at random. Find the probability that the pupil takes

(a) art or music, [1]

(b) both art and music, [2]

(c) exactly one of the two subjects, [1]

(d) music but not art. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n(\text{art or music}) = 120 - 20 = 100$, so $P = \dfrac{100}{120} = \dfrac{5}{6}$.

(b) $n(\text{both}) = 70 + 55 - 100 = 25$, so $P(\text{both}) = \dfrac{25}{120} = \dfrac{5}{24}$.

(c) Exactly one: $100 - 25 = 75$ pupils, so $P = \dfrac{75}{120} = \dfrac{5}{8}$.

(d) Music but not art: $55 - 25 = 30$ pupils, so $P = \dfrac{30}{120} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.solution_md: The pupils taking neither give the union; the addition theorem in counting form then gives the overlap.

questions.stem_md:
A number is chosen at random from $1, 2, \dots, 50$. Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be the events "a multiple of $2$", "a multiple of $5$" and "a multiple of $7$". Find

(a) $P(A \cup B)$, [2]

(b) $P(A \cup B \cup C)$, using $P(A \cup B \cup C) = \sum P(A) - \sum P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap B \cap C)$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A \cap B$ is the multiples of $10$: $10, 20, 30, 40, 50$, so $n(A \cap B) = 5$. Then $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{25}{50} + \dfrac{10}{50} - \dfrac{5}{50} = \dfrac{30}{50} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

(b) $n(A) = 25$, $n(B) = 10$, $n(C) = 7$. The pair overlaps are the multiples of $10$, $14$ and $35$: $n(A \cap B) = 5$, $n(A \cap C) = 3$ ($14, 28, 42$) and $n(B \cap C) = 1$ ($35$). The multiples of $70$ do not occur up to $50$, so $n(A \cap B \cap C) = 0$.
$P(A \cup B \cup C) = \dfrac{25 + 10 + 7}{50} - \dfrac{5 + 3 + 1}{50} + \dfrac{0}{50} = \dfrac{42 - 9 + 0}{50} = \dfrac{33}{50} = \dfrac{33}{50}$.

questions.solution_md: Find every overlap count first; the multiples of 70 do not occur up to 50, so the triple overlap is empty.

questions.stem_md:
A coin is tossed. If it shows heads, a four-sided die with faces $1$ to $4$ is rolled; if it shows tails, the coin is tossed once more. The outcomes $\mathrm{H1}, \mathrm{H2}, \mathrm{H3}, \mathrm{H4}, \mathrm{TH}, \mathrm{TT}$ are given the probabilities $\dfrac{1}{8}, \dfrac{1}{8}, \dfrac{1}{8}, \dfrac{1}{8}, \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{1}{4}$. Let $A$ be "at least one head appears" and $B$ "at least one tail appears". Find

(a) a check that the assignment is valid, [1]

(b) $P(A)$, [1]

(c) $P(B)$, [1]

(d) $P(A \cap B)$ and $P(A \cup B)$ by the addition theorem. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) All six values are positive and $4 \times \dfrac{1}{8} + 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1$, so the assignment is valid.

(b) $A = \{\mathrm{H1}, \mathrm{H2}, \mathrm{H3}, \mathrm{H4}, \mathrm{TH}\}$, so $P(A) = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

(c) $B = \{\mathrm{TH}, \mathrm{TT}\}$, so $P(B) = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

(d) The only outcome in both is $\mathrm{TH}$, so $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{4}$. Then $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} = 1$, which is correct because every outcome has a head or a tail.
